chunks: As for their assertion that this amounts to procuring grace for someone else, it is incorrect.

Because we say, each person who helps the Imam and strengthens his rule, enjoys a benefit specific for himself, may it carry expediency for others as well. It is like what you say about the apostles that their carriage of the burden of Prophethood and delivery of message to the public bears expediency for others, because for them in doing so is a benefit specific to them, even if it contains benefit for others.

This requires the opponent to answer a query about “those having a say” - how is it that it is obligatory on them to choose an Imam for expediencies that encompass the entire Ummah and is it not requiring one to do something that benefits someone else? Whatever may be your justification with regard to the situation of the apostles is our very answer here.
ai.seo_question: Why is choosing an Imam considered a benefit for the people themselves and not just for the Imam?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi refutes the notion that appointing an Imam is merely a favor to the community by arguing that the obligation of *nusrat al-imam* (supporting the Imam) serves the self-interest of the people, similar to how Prophets benefit themselves through their mission. He extends this logic to the *Ahl al-Hall wa-l-Aqd* (those who bind and loose), asserting that their selection of the Imam is an act of self-benefit rather than a duty performed solely for the sake of others, thereby establishing a consistent theological framework for communal obligation.
